cases.question: What has he learned from AI systems failing?
failures: expected at least one cited claim, got none
cases.answer:
Four documented failures anchor this, all from the Ballards Platform work where Josh runs an AI coding agent as a collaborator under written standards: (1) health checks reported failure against services that were actually healthy, because localhost resolved to IPv6 inside containers while services listened on IPv4; (2) a preflight script meant to catch committed private keys detected nothing, because its pattern was swallowed as command options rather than matched; (3) an authentication test passed without proving anything, because it compared a container's token against that same container's own running config; (4) the coding agent printed a live service token into the session while verifying documentation.

The pattern Josh draws from these: every one of them looked like a success first. That's the stated reason he now builds verification into systems rather than trusting output that looks confident. The token leak specifically pushed him toward a systemic fix rather than a one-off patch.

This happened on a private system, so it's self-reported — no public repo or logs an outside party can check.</answer>

cases.question: What's his infrastructure background?
failures: expected at least one cited claim, got none
cases.answer:
Thirteen years, all on-premises, across five roles:

- Current (2022–present), Principal Systems Administrator, defense contractor: primary admin for a production VMware environment — 24 ESXi hosts, 100+ VMs. Built VMware Cloud Foundation 5.2.2 from scratch, migrated vSphere 7 to 8 with no data loss, hand-applied STIGs across every component, owns daily security operations (vulnerability scanning, remediation, POA&M tracking), runs Linux BIND DNS.
- Northrop Grumman (2022, 9 months): Windows infrastructure across 3 networks / 5 sites / ~300 users. Rebuilt imaging (WDS/MDT) and patching (WSUS/WAM), stood up Nessus vulnerability scanning, administered NetApp storage, mentored two L2 admins.
- GE Aviation (2016–2021, 4 years): kept 300+ HPC cluster nodes available, ran a migration off Windows 7 / RHEL 5-6 onto Windows 10 / RHEL 7, trained a helpdesk team and led a deployment team across networking, storage, VMware, Linux — then moved into owning the product side of that same tooling.
- Etegent Technologies (2021–2022): IT manager for a small engineering firm, isolated-network compliance (ISSO), built the company's first IT budget from nothing.
- US Marine Corps (2012–2016): Cyber Network Operator — built and maintained 1,000+ Active Directory accounts and group policy, stood up networks alongside foreign militaries, supervised 12 Marines.

The honest gap: all of it is on-premises — virtualization, storage, Windows/Linux, security hardening. No AWS/GCP/Kubernetes at professional scale, no service with external customers, no on-call rotation for elastic scaling. That's a real mismatch with the infrastructure problems an AI startup usually has (elastic compute, inference cost, queueing). What transfers is the discipline — hardening every component individually, completing a hypervisor migration without losing data, running something people depend on — not the platform itself. Whether that transfers fast enough is a fair thing to test in a conversation, not something the record settles.

All of this is self-reported work history, not independently checkable in the way the public GitHub projects are.</answer>

cases.question: Why Naive?
failures: expected at least one cited claim, got none
cases.answer:
Naive builds autonomous companies, which forces a question Josh has been circling for about a year on his own: what can an agent do unsupervised, what needs a human sign-off, and how does anyone check afterward.

A few specific things pulled him toward this role:

**The Account Kit and this application are the same kind of object.** Naive's public starter template governs an agent by declaring, outside the agent, what it may touch. This application does the same with a compiled evidence artifact and a nine-tool registry the agent can't reach past. Josh built his before reading Naive's — finding the same shape twice reads to him as the problem forcing the solution.

**He wrote a governing document before he knew that was a pattern.** The standards file constraining his coding agent on his personal platform project is the same species of artifact as a product constitution: it constrains behavior rather than directing tasks.

**Both systems land consequential agent actions in the same state.** Naive's approvals queue holds sensitive actions as pending until a human acts. This application's only write returns pending_human_approval. Nobody coordinated that.

**Repeatability is the question he most wants answered and doesn't have an answer to.** Every documented failure he's had building with AI reported success first — a health check, a security script, a passing test, all wrong about what they actually proved. How a company running agents at volume gets the same work to produce the same result twice is the first thing he'd ask.

Separately, and worth stating plainly rather than late: the role is listed on-site in San Francisco, Josh is in Ohio, and he is not relocating. That is independent of whether the reasoning above is compelling.</answer>

cases.question: What experience does he have with agents?
cases.answer:
Two distinct kinds of "agent experience," and it's worth separating them.

1. Using a coding agent as a daily collaborator. On Ballards Platform (a private family system), Josh spent roughly a year building and operating real software — Docker services, a Flask API, a Paper plugin, GitHub workflows — with an AI coding agent doing the writing, under a set of engineering standards, verification rules, and human-review boundaries he wrote himself. Four documented failures came out of that work (a health check lied about IPv4/IPv6, a security-check regex was silently broken, a test that couldn't fail, and an agent that printed a live credential into the session). Those failures are why he now builds verification into the system rather than trusting the agent's confidence.

2. This application itself is a small live agent system: one agent, nine narrow read-only tools plus one gated write, a build gate with five stages (schema, approval, privacy linting, cross-reference integrity, content hash), and a server-side verifier that rejects unsupported claims. That's real tool-use and structured-output experience, built in about two days.

What's not there: multi-agent orchestration. He has not built or operated a system where multiple agents coordinate, has not authored an MCP server, and has no agent runtime running unattended in production where something depended on the result. The role-fit rubric marks this as a clean GAP — the cleanest one against the posting — and marks the broader "agent runtimes / MCP" nice-to-have as PARTIAL: familiar as a heavy user and rule-writer, not as a builder of the runtime itself.

So: real, sustained, hands-on experience directing and governing an agent, plus one working (small-scale) agentic system built for this application. No multi-agent or orchestration experience at all.

cases.question: How does he think about human-in-the-loop systems?
cases.answer:
Josh's view has an explicit revision in it, which is the most telling part.

He used to think human review added value by editing the work — catching things line by line, commenting, improving. He changed his mind: the human's job is to underwrite the outcome, not to add material comment. If a reviewer keeps having substantive things to say, that's a signal something upstream (context, standards, spec) is broken — not evidence the review step is working as intended. He arrived at this after studying how agent-driven work operates at higher volume than his own small-PR practice, and he wrote it down as something he'd gotten wrong rather than quietly updating.

That view is backed by a harder lesson: every documented failure he's had building with AI looked like a success first — a health check that reported healthy while services were down, a test that passed without proving anything, a security scanner that found nothing because its pattern was silently broken, a credential printed into a session during a "verification" step. None of these were caught by confidence. They were caught, when they were caught, by someone going and checking. That's why he now designs for verification rather than trusting a system's self-report — this application itself computes its fit verdict server-side and rejects any claim marked SUPPORTED that can't name a record.

On where the human sits structurally: he treats a human-in-the-loop boundary as something declared outside the agent, before it runs, not a behavior the agent is instructed into. The only consequential action this application can take returns a pending-human-approval state rather than executing — same shape as an approvals queue holding sensitive actions until a person acts. He built that pattern independently, before he'd read Naive's own template, which is a coincidence he thinks is worth a conversation rather than evidence of anything more.</answer>
